details:
**Haman**
The book's villain, an Agagite (a descendant of the Amalekite king Agag) who serves as the Persian king's chief minister. Angered that Mordecai will not bow to him, he plots to exterminate all the Jews of the empire, but he is ruined when the king finds him "falling on the couch" where Esther lay while begging her for mercy, and he is hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai.

**Vashti**
The first queen of King Ahasuerus, who refuses his command to appear at a drunken banquet wearing the "crown royal" to display her beauty (in rabbinic tradition, wearing only the crown). She is deposed, the king sends out a decree that "every man should bear rule in his own house," and a search for a new queen begins, with the candidates given a year of beauty treatments with myrrh and perfumes under the eunuch Hegai.

**Mordecai**
Esther's cousin, often described as her uncle, who raised her after her parents died. He refuses to bow to Haman, uncovers a plot against the king, urges Esther to intervene for her people, and is ultimately made the king's chief minister in Haman's place.

**Ahasuerus**
The Persian king who makes Esther his queen, usually identified with Xerxes I. He grants Haman permission to destroy the Jews, but later lets Mordecai issue a counter-edict allowing the Jews to defend themselves.

**Bigthan and Teresh**
Two of the king's eunuch guards who plot to assassinate Ahasuerus. Mordecai uncovers the plot, they are hanged, and the deed is recorded in the royal chronicles; when the sleepless king later has the chronicles read to him, he orders Haman to publicly honor Mordecai.

**No mention of God**
Esther is one of only two books of the Hebrew Bible, along with the Song of Songs, that never explicitly mentions God. The Greek version of Esther includes added passages with prayers that mention God.

**Purim and the casting of lots**
The joyous Jewish holiday that celebrates the deliverance of the Jews from Haman's plot, and the occasion on which the Book of Esther is read aloud. Its name comes from pur, the "lot" Haman cast to choose the date of the massacre, the 13th of the month Adar.

**Fifty-cubit gallows**
The gallows (or impaling pole), about 75 feet high, that Haman builds on the advice of his wife Zeresh in order to hang Mordecai. Haman himself is hanged on it instead.

**Esther approaches the king unsummoned**
After fasting for three days, Esther risks death by going to the king without being called, but he extends his golden scepter and promises her any request "even to the half of the kingdom." At banquets she prefaces her requests with "if it please the king" and reveals that she is Jewish and that Haman plans to destroy her people.

**"For such a time as this"**
Mordecai's words to Esther when she hesitates to approach the king: "who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" The phrase is often quoted as a call to action.

**Hadassah**
Esther's Hebrew name, meaning "myrtle." "Esther" is her Persian name.

**Graggers (groggers)**
Noisemakers that Jews shake, along with booing and stamping, to drown out Haman's name every time it is read aloud from the Megillah on Purim.

**Shushan (Susa)**
The Persian capital where the story is set. Shushan Purim, celebrated a day later in walled cities such as Jerusalem, is named for it.

**Megillah**
The Hebrew name for the scroll of Esther (Megillat Esther), the best known of the five "megillot" (scrolls) of the Hebrew Bible. The rare cantillation marks yerach ben yomo and qarnei farah appear together on a single word in it.

**Babylonian deity names**
Some scholars note that the names Mordecai and Esther resemble those of the Babylonian gods Marduk and Ishtar. Combined with the book's lack of reference to God, this has led some to read it as an allegory or as adapted from older Mesopotamian material.
